title: Risk factors associated with lower extremity stress fractures in runners: a systematic review with meta-analysis
authors: Wright AA, Taylor JB, Ford KR, Siska L, Smoliga JM
population: Runners in 8 eligible studies (4 pooled in the meta-analysis); search through 9 January 2014
findings: Stress fractures account for 15-20% of all musculoskeletal injuries in runners, with up to 95% in the lower extremities.
8 articles met inclusion criteria (7 considered low risk of bias); 4 qualified for meta-analysis.
Previous history of stress fracture: pooled OR 4.99 (95% CI 2.91-8.56; p<0.001; I2 = 0%).
Female sex: pooled OR 2.31 (95% CI 1.24-4.29; p<0.01; I2 = 0%).
Only previous stress fracture and female sex are risk factors strongly supported by the data.
limitations: Only four studies pooled; search ended January 2014; observational data. Abstract does not give weekly-volume or energy-availability findings, so no training threshold follows.
implications: A previous bone stress injury should trigger a markedly more conservative profile and a prompt to consult a clinician; the specific step sizes are engineering defaults.
Female sex modifies bone-stress vigilance (surface low-energy-availability and menstrual warning signs), not overall volume caps (see Hollander 2021).
No numeric volume threshold is supported by this paper.

verification.notes: Crossref: BJSM 49:1517-1523 (online Jul 2015). Abstract matched; p-values and I2 confirmed from the raw record. Removed the researcher's unsupported remark about energy availability and BMD from limitations.
